subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Reading a described table: separating total revenue, sales volume and revenue per unit
learning_objective: Extract a derived per-unit quantity from a table and distinguish it from raw totals, rejecting statements that conflate sales volume, total revenue and revenue per unit.
question:
A publisher records the following figures for its four book formats in a single year:

| Format    | Copies sold (thousands) | Revenue (€ thousands) |
|-----------|-------------------------|------------------------|
| Hardback  | 40                      | 800                    |
| Paperback | 120                     | 1,080                  |
| E-book    | 200                     | 1,000                  |
| Audiobook | 25                      | 500                    |

On the basis of these figures alone, which of the following statements must be true?

choices.A: Audiobooks were the least profitable format because they sold the fewest copies.
choices.B: The format with the highest sales volume also earned the highest total revenue.
choices.C: E-books generated the highest total revenue of the four formats.
choices.D: Paperbacks earned more revenue per copy sold than hardbacks did.
choices.E: Hardbacks and audiobooks earned the same average revenue per copy sold.

explanation: Revenue per copy = revenue ÷ copies. Hardback: 800/40 = €20; Paperback: 1,080/120 = €9; E-book: 1,000/200 = €5; Audiobook: 500/25 = €20. So hardbacks and audiobooks share the same per-copy figure (€20). Checking the rest: total revenue is highest for paperbacks (1,080 > 1,000), while sales volume is highest for e-books (200) — the volume leader and the revenue leader are different formats. 'Profit' cannot be found at all because no cost data are given. The key skill is separating three different quantities — total revenue, units sold and revenue per unit — that the distractors deliberately blur.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: profitability cannot be judged without cost data, and audiobooks actually have a high per-copy revenue (€20). It encodes the misconception that the lowest sales volume implies the lowest profit.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: e-books have the highest volume (200k) but paperbacks have the highest revenue (€1,080k), so the two rankings do not coincide. It reflects conflating sales-volume rank with revenue rank.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: e-books earned €1,000k, but paperbacks earned €1,080k, so paperbacks lead on revenue. This encodes the misconception that the highest-volume format (e-books, 200k copies) automatically earns the most revenue.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: paperbacks earn €9 per copy versus €20 for hardbacks, so hardbacks earn far more per copy. This mistakes higher total revenue (1,080 > 800) for higher revenue per unit.
option_analysis.E: Correct: 800/40 = €20 per copy for hardbacks and 500/25 = €20 per copy for audiobooks, so their average revenue per copy is identical.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: System reliability: combining independent probabilities across series and parallel components
learning_objective: Compute the operating probability of a system with a required (series) component and a redundant (parallel) pair, correctly applying the complement rule to the 'at least one' subsystem.
question: A cooling system operates only if its controller is working AND at least one of its two backup pumps is working. The controller works with probability 0.90. Each pump works with probability 0.80. The controller and the two pumps fail independently of one another. What is the probability that the cooling system operates?
explanation: The two pumps form a redundant (parallel) pair: the pump subsystem works unless BOTH pumps fail. P(both pumps fail) = 0.20 × 0.20 = 0.04, so P(at least one pump works) = 1 − 0.04 = 0.96. The controller is in series (it is required), so multiply: P(system) = 0.90 × 0.96 = 0.864. The core reasoning is recognising that 'at least one of two' is handled by the complement of joint failure, and that a required component multiplies the result rather than adding to it.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 1 − (0.2)(0.2) = 0.960 is only the pump subsystem's reliability; it omits the required controller factor of 0.90.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 1 − (0.10)(0.20)(0.20) = 0.996 treats every component, including the controller, as redundant/parallel, i.e. it wrongly assumes the system works if ANY single component works.
option_analysis.C: Correct: P(at least one pump) = 1 − (0.2)(0.2) = 0.96; combined with the required controller, 0.90 × 0.96 = 0.864.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.720 counts only a single pump and ignores the backup pump entirely, discarding the redundancy.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.80 = 0.576 treats the two pumps as if BOTH were required (a series pair), ignoring the redundancy that only one pump need work.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Categorical syllogism (Darii): valid conclusion versus illicit conversion and over-generalisation
learning_objective: Identify the single conclusion guaranteed by an 'all' premise combined with a 'some' premise, while rejecting over-generalisation, illicit conversion and unsupported negative inferences.
question:
Consider the following two statements, both taken to be true:

1. All professional athletes follow a strict diet.
2. Some members of this gym are professional athletes.

Which one of the following conclusions is logically guaranteed by these two statements together?

choices.A: Everyone who follows a strict diet is a professional athlete.
choices.B: At least one member of this gym follows a strict diet.
choices.C: Some members of this gym do not follow a strict diet.
choices.D: No member of this gym who follows a strict diet is a professional athlete.
choices.E: Every member of this gym follows a strict diet.

explanation: This is the valid form 'All M are P; some S are M; therefore some S are P.' The gym members who are professional athletes (guaranteed to exist by statement 2) must, by statement 1, follow a strict diet. Hence at least one gym member follows a strict diet. Each other option fails: 'some' cannot be strengthened to 'all'; an 'All A are B' premise cannot be reversed into 'All B are A'; and no negative conclusion about the remaining gym members can be drawn, because their diet status is simply unknown.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: from 'all athletes follow a strict diet' one cannot infer that all diet-followers are athletes — this is the illicit conversion of an 'All A are B' statement into 'All B are A'.
option_analysis.B: Correct: the gym members who are athletes exist and must follow a strict diet, so at least one gym member follows a strict diet (the valid Darii conclusion).
option_analysis.C: Wrong: nothing is stated about the non-athlete gym members' diets, so a negative conclusion is unsupported; this is inferring a negative from premises that license none.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: the athlete gym members both follow a strict diet AND are athletes, so this overlap must exist; the statement denies a case that is guaranteed to occur.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: statement 2 says only that SOME gym members are athletes, so nothing follows about every member. This is the over-generalisation of 'some' to 'all'.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Weakening a causal claim by reverse causation (the effect drives the supposed cause)
learning_objective: Select the option that most undermines a cause-and-effect conclusion drawn from a correlation by reversing the proposed causal direction, distinguishing it from irrelevant, strengthening or merely descriptive facts.
question: In a survey of coastal towns, those that had installed the most public security cameras over the previous decade also reported the highest numbers of thefts. A columnist concluded that installing security cameras causes the number of thefts to rise. Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the columnist's conclusion?

choices.A: Local councils typically approve funding for extra cameras only after a documented surge in thefts.
choices.B: Towns that installed no cameras reported little change in their theft figures over the same decade.
choices.C: Opinion surveys show that most residents support the continued use of public security cameras.
choices.D: Security cameras have become considerably cheaper and easier to install over the past ten years.
choices.E: Camera footage has enabled the police to arrest a greater proportion of thieves than before.

explanation: The columnist infers causation (cameras → more thefts) from a correlation. The strongest weakener reverses the causal arrow: if councils install extra cameras only in response to thefts that have already surged, then rising theft causes the cameras, not the other way round, and the correlation is fully explained without the columnist's causal claim. The other options are irrelevant (cost, public opinion), concern a different outcome (arrest rates), or actually reinforce the correlation rather than undermine the causal interpretation.

option_analysis.A: Correct: if extra cameras are installed only after thefts have already surged, the causal direction is reversed — pre-existing theft drives camera installation — so the data no longer support 'cameras cause thefts'.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: no change in theft where there are no cameras, alongside high theft where there are many, tends to STRENGTHEN the correlation the columnist relies on rather than weaken the causal conclusion.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: residents' approval of cameras is about opinion, not about the causal relationship between cameras and theft rates; it is irrelevant.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: the falling cost of cameras is irrelevant to whether cameras cause thefts; it says nothing about the direction or existence of a causal link.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: higher arrest rates concern how many thieves are caught, not whether cameras increase the number of thefts committed; it leaves the causal claim untouched.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Average speed as a time-weighted (harmonic) mean: the unattainable round-trip target
learning_objective: Recognise that average speed over a fixed distance is total distance divided by total time (not the arithmetic mean of leg speeds), and deduce when a target round-trip average is unattainable at any finite speed.
question: On a mountain road, a cyclist rides from the base to the summit at a steady 20 km/h. She then returns down the same road to the base. She wants her average speed for the whole round trip to be 40 km/h. What speed must she maintain on the descent to achieve this?

choices.D: No finite descending speed can achieve this.

explanation: Average speed for the whole trip = total distance ÷ total time. Let the one-way distance be d. To average 40 km/h over the round trip (2d), the total time must be 2d/40 = d/20. But the ascent at 20 km/h already takes d/20 — the entire time budget. That leaves zero time for the descent, which would require infinite speed. Because the slow ascent consumes all the time a 40 km/h average would allow, no finite descent speed can reach the target. This exposes the trap of averaging leg speeds arithmetically: over equal distances, average speed is the time-weighted (harmonic) mean, which is dominated by the slower leg.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 40 km/h assumes the descent speed simply equals the desired average, ignoring that the slow ascent has already pulled the overall time far beyond what a 40 km/h average permits.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 60 km/h comes from setting the arithmetic mean of the two leg speeds equal to 40, i.e. (20 + x)/2 = 40. Average speed over equal distances is not the arithmetic mean of the leg speeds.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: 80 km/h comes from reasoning that because the target (40) is double the ascent speed (20), the descent must be double the target; this is a spurious proportionality.
option_analysis.D: Correct: the ascent at 20 km/h already uses the full time budget (d/20) that a 40 km/h round-trip average allows, so the descent would need zero time, i.e. an infinite speed — no finite speed works.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 120 km/h is an arbitrary large but finite value chosen on the belief that a sufficiently high speed can always reach any average, missing that the time constraint makes the target unattainable at any finite speed.
